name: GPUs & AI accelerators
summary: Chips built to do enormous numbers of simple multiplications in parallel, the core operation of neural networks.

text: A normal computer brain (a CPU) is like one very clever person doing sums one after another. A GPU is like a stadium full of people each doing one small sum at the same time.
AI needs billions of small sums, so the stadium wins.
D1.analogy: One clever person versus a stadium full of helpers.

text: Neural networks mostly multiply large grids of numbers (matrices). GPUs and other accelerators contain thousands of simple cores and specialised matrix units that do these multiplications in parallel.
They also use lower-precision number formats (16-, 8- or even 4-bit) to fit more maths per second and more numbers in memory.
Software platforms such as CUDA or ROCm let frameworks like PyTorch use the hardware without chip-level code.

columns.title: GPU / accelerator

D2.analogy: A CPU is a few expert chefs; a GPU is a huge team of line cooks all chopping at once.
D2.analogyBreaks: Line cooks work independently. GPU cores run the same instruction on different data in lockstep, so work that can't be split evenly wastes most of the team.

predict.question: Which kind of work benefits most from a GPU?
options: One long chain of steps where each depends on the last
predict.explanation: GPUs win when the same operation applies to lots of data at once, which is exactly what matrix multiplication is.

text: Frontier questions: specialised inference chips versus general-purpose GPUs, how far low-precision formats can go without hurting quality, and whether memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic becomes the permanent bottleneck.

sources.title: Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr From First Principles (Horace He)
